data.title: Brahman, Atman, and the Cycle of Rebirth
data.sourcePassage: Hinduism — or Sanatana Dharma, the Eternal Way — is one of the world's oldest religions. At its heart is the concept of Brahman: the ultimate reality, the source of all existence, infinite and beyond full human comprehension. Brahman is not simply a god among gods but the underlying reality of everything. Each person possesses an atman — an individual soul or true inner self — which many Hindu traditions teach is ultimately connected to or even identical with Brahman. The atman is eternal: it is not destroyed when the body dies. Instead, it passes through samsara — the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. The quality of each new life is shaped by karma, the moral law of cause and effect: actions, intentions, and choices in this life have consequences in future lives. The ultimate goal is moksha — liberation from the cycle of samsara — when the atman is freed and returns to or merges with Brahman.

data.title: Puja and the Mandir
data.sourcePassage: Puja is the central act of Hindu worship — showing devotion, love, and respect to a deity through rituals. Puja can take place at home or in a mandir (temple). At home, a family shrine holds one or more murti — sacred images or representations of deities. Worshippers offer flowers, incense, water, food (prasad), and a flame (aarti). The bell is rung to invite the deity's attention, and mantras such as 'Om' are recited. In the mandir, a pujari (priest) performs more formal worship: the murti is bathed, dressed, and given offerings as if honouring a royal guest. Aarti — the waving of a flame before the deity — is performed several times daily. Worshippers come for darshan: the auspicious 'seeing' of the deity, a sacred moment of connection. The mandir layout includes a main shrine room, separate shrines for different deities, and a washing area. Shoes are always removed before entering.

data.title: Diwali, Holi, and Hindu Ethics
data.sourcePassage: Hindu festivals mark important moments in the religious calendar and connect worshippers to the stories, deities, and values of their tradition. Diwali — the Festival of Lights — celebrates the return of Rama and Sita after Rama's defeat of the demon king Ravana. People light diyas (clay lamps), set off fireworks, share sweets, and perform puja for Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. The lights symbolise the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance. Holi, the spring festival, celebrates the victory of good over evil — connected to the story of the faithful boy Prahlad — and is marked by joyful throwing of coloured powder and water. Hindu ethics are shaped by key principles: ahimsa (non-violence) encourages respect for all living beings and is expressed through vegetarianism; dharma means fulfilling one's duties and living according to one's role; sewa means selfless service to others; and satya means truthfulness. Together these principles guide how Hindus live in family, community, and the wider world.
